newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul shrs end lower for three days on Sammi woes.
newsitem.headline: Seoul shrs end lower for three days on Sammi woes.

text.p: Seoul stocks closed sharply lower on Friday as the Sammi Group's failure fuelled fears of a possibility of more defaults, brokers said.
They said the market was further dented by Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik's remarks that companies that cannot stand by themselves should be liquidated.
The composite stock index lost 2.37 percent, or 15.23 points, to 627.63.
"I don't know how long the Sammi jitters will affect the market. Investors are at their wits' end," said broker Kim Duck-sun of Hyundai Securities.
Minister Kang told business leaders: "We must bravely liquidate companies that are operating on margins."
"Investors are fearful as they believe other groups, not as big as Sammi, will also default," said Lee Hee-myung of Samsung Securities. "The underlying market sentiment is at its worst."
Brokers said domestic banks were trying to recall their loans to smaller companies, most of them are said to be vulnerable to the effects of tightening credit.
The market was also hit by jitters about the possibility of a financial crisis. Benchmark yields on three-year corporate bonds hit a new 18-month high of 12.89 percent.
Brokers said across the board selling orders dragged down 687 shares. Out of the decliners, 183 stocks sank to their maximum permitted daily limit of eight percent.
No quick recovery is seen in financial shares as the Sammi troubles renewed concerns about their accumulated bad debts. The financial sub-index lost 4.92 percent to 429.86.

Korea First Bank, a major creditor to Sammi Steel, went to its limit and year low of 2,670 won. Sammi Corp's creditor, Commercial Bank of Korea, also closed at its daily lower limit to 3,440. The banks' share prices are far off their face value of 5,000 won.

Coryo Securities, a payment guarantor to Sammi Steel, fell to a new year low of 4,000 won. Another guarantor Dongsuh Securities hit its daily lower limit of eight percent 400 won to 4,600, a fresh 1997 bottom.

Disappointment from a government economic package also overshadowed the market. Many investors anticipated an announcement of an earlier than planned raise in the foreign stock ownerhip ceiling, which they believe would lure foreign funds into the market.
But Minister Kang said on Wednesday he had not considered such matters at all.
The government has said it would raise the stock investment ceiling to 23 percent from 20 percent some time this year, but a schedule has not yet been set.
"I'm not sure how much foreign funds would flow into the market with the limit expansion," Lee said. "Foreign investors are reluctant to accumulate shares right now."
The Securities Supervisory Board said foreign investors sold 3.8 million banking shares out of the total 5.36 million share sold on Friday.
Brokers said the market would soon breach the psychological 600 level and head for the 550 mark. -- Yeom Yoon-jeong
